newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria has no answers to bomb attacks - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Algeria has no answers to bomb attacks - analysts.

text.p: Algerians, diplomats and analysts in Algiers said on Saturday that President Liamine Zeroual's vow to the nation to end "terrorism" shed no light on a way out of violence which has killed more than 200 people in two weeks.

Zeroual, speaking on state television on Friday, largely blamed "foreign circles" for manipulating those he called "criminals, traitors and mercenaries" -- the authorities' terms for Moslem fundamentalists.

Omar Belhouchet, editor of El Watan, said: "Those who expected new and innovative decisions, or a deeper analysis on the nature of the crisis and formulation of a political vision to give real hope to a disillusioned people, all risk to be disappointed."

Belhouchet, who has escaped at least one assassination attempt and has been brought before Algerian courts for his newspaper's reporting, added: "To mobilise the people, words are certainly important but are not enough."
One diplomatic source in Algiers, which has been blasted by at least five bombs in a week, said: "It (the speech) was long on condemnation but short on answers."
Another described it as a "bit of an anti-climax" for foreign capitals which had expected something more solid, "a view not widely shared by Algerians and people here."
The Arabic-language El Khabar said Zeroual's address to Algeria's 29 million people "brought no new initiative or new measure" to end the violence. Liberte expressed the same view.

Zeroual's 20-minute prepared speech closed what newspapers termed a bloody weekend, with massacres in which Le Matin said 59 people had been killed, and other independent papers reported variously 26 people and 29.
Residents on Friday said at least 15 people, 10 of them women, had been slaughtered in one attack on the outskirts of the capital overnight. Their throats had been slit, and many had been mutilated.
Well over 400 people have been killed since November, with more than 200 of them in the first half of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan which started on January 10.
The Armed Islamic Group (GIA), the most feared of the rebel groups born during five years of conflict in which about 60,000 people have died, had vowed to increase attacks in Ramadan.
"The war will continue and will be intensified during the month of Ramadan," GIA leader Antar Zouabri said in a statement posted on mosque walls.

Zeroual, who gave no details of the killings or steps to increase security, said: "...innocent citizens, of all categories, are victims each day of a blind terrorism never equalled in other times or other places."
He gave no date for a general election promised for the first half of this year, saying only that Algeria would pursue its path to pluralism and democracy.
But he also criciticed what he termed "voices" inside Algeria -- a reference to legal opposition politicians -- that they were trying in vain to hinder Algeria's march to recovery.
The scrapping by the authorities in January 1992 of the last general election, dominated by Islamists, sparked the violence which has continued unabated for five years.
"I confirm to the dear Algerian people the determination of the Algerian state to battle against the terrorist groups until their final eradication," he said.
Zeroual gave no names of countries he said were involved.

Early in the conflict, Algiers accused Iran and Sudan of backing armed fundamentalists. Officials have also expressed anger at German asylum being granted to Rabah Kebir, a former leader of the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).

The Algerian official news agency APS, in a report just ahead of Zeroual's speech, quoted Algeria's ambassador to Spain as saying Iran had always "morally and materially supported the terrorists" but would fail in exporting its Islamist model.
